question: What is the primary anatomical definition of a joint?

options.A: The point of contact between bones
options.B: A bundle of fibers connecting muscle to bone
options.C: A fluid-filled cavity inside skeletal muscle
options.D: The protective cushion at the end of a long bone

explanation: A joint is anatomically defined as any place where adjacent bones meet or make contact. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T6#GNS121_U3_T6_h1)

question: Why do joints that move a lot tend to be less stable?

options.A: Constant synovial fluid production softens the surrounding bone matrix over time
options.B: Ligaments must remain loose to allow muscles to pull bones in multiple directions
options.C: Thick cartilage layers prevent bones from locking into place during heavy physical activity
options.D: Bone shapes and shallow sockets allow a wide range of motion but increase dislocation risk

explanation: Greater freedom of movement in a joint requires less bony containment, which makes it easier for the joint to get displaced. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T6#GNS121_U3_T6_h1)

question: A freely movable joint is functionally classified by which medical term?
explanation: Diarthroses are freely movable joints found predominantly in the appendicular skeleton. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T6#GNS121_U3_T6_h2)

question: How do structural and functional classifications of joints differ?

options.A: Structural classification applies only to upper limbs, whereas functional applies to the spine
options.B: Structural classification relies on binding materials, whereas functional relies on movement degree
options.C: Functional classification uses Latin prefixes, whereas structural uses common English terms
options.D: Functional classification measures bone length, while structural measures joint cavity size

explanation: The structural system groups joints by what connects them (fibrous, cartilaginous, synovial), while the functional system groups them by how much they move. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T6#GNS121_U3_T6_h2)

question: What type of fibrous joint holds a tooth firmly in its jaw socket?
explanation: A gomphosis is a specialized peg-in-socket fibrous joint securing teeth within the maxilla and mandible. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T6#GNS121_U3_T6_h3)

question: A patient injures the joint between the lower leg bones just above the ankle, affecting slight give. Which joint structure is this?
explanation: The connection between the distal tibia and fibula is a syndesmosis, where bones are bound by longer ligaments that allow just a little movement. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T6#GNS121_U3_T6_h3)

question: Which cartilage type primarily connects the bones in a symphysis joint?
explanation: Symphyses feature pads of fibrocartilage that act as shock absorbers while permitting limited movement. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T6#GNS121_U3_T6_h4)

question: What happens to a growth plate joint (synchondrosis) in a child when they finish growing?

options.A: It transforms into a fibrocartilaginous symphysis pad
options.B: It dissolves entirely to allow bone marrow expansion
options.C: It develops a synovial capsule to increase limb mobility
options.D: It turns into solid bone and becomes an immovable joint

explanation: Temporary growth plates turn into solid bone once a person stops growing, converting the joint into an immobile connection. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T6#GNS121_U3_T6_h4)

question: What is the primary function of synovial fluid inside a joint cavity?

options.A: Lubrication and nutrient supply to cartilage
options.B: Regulating core body temperature during exercise
options.C: Anchoring muscles directly to opposing bone surfaces
options.D: Preventing blood flow to the joint capsule

explanation: Because articular cartilage lacks its own blood supply, synovial fluid provides essential nourishment and reduces friction during movement. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T6#GNS121_U3_T6_h5)

question: Which layer of the joint capsule produces synovial fluid?
explanation: The inner layer of the joint capsule is the synovial membrane, which lines the joint cavity and secretes the lubricating fluid. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T6#GNS121_U3_T6_h5)

question: Which synovial joint subtype is exemplified by the shoulder and hip?
explanation: The shoulder and hip are ball-and-socket joints, allowing multiaxial movement across multiple planes. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T6#GNS121_U3_T6_h6)

question: How does a hinge joint restrict movement compared to a ball-and-socket joint?

options.A: It allows rotation along a vertical axis exclusively
options.B: It permits motion in only one single plane
options.C: It relies entirely on fibrous connective tissue bands
options.D: It lacks a synovial cavity to prevent dislocation

explanation: Hinge joints work like a door hinge, restricting movement to bending and straightening in just one direction. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T6#GNS121_U3_T6_h6)

question: What term describes moving a limb away from the midline of the body?
explanation: Abduction is the movement of a body part away from the median plane of the body. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T6#GNS121_U3_T6_h7)

question: A patient points their toes downward toward the floor. Which ankle movement has occurred?
explanation: Lifting the heel or pointing the toes downward is plantar flexion, whereas lifting the foot upward is dorsiflexion. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T6#GNS121_U3_T6_h7)

question: Which type of arthritis is an autoimmune condition that attacks the joint lining?
explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis happens when the immune system attacks the joint lining, causing long-term inflammation and joint damage. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T6#GNS121_U3_T6_h8)

question: What is the main cause of joint damage in osteoarthritis?

options.A: Crystal deposits of uric acid settling in the synovial fluid
options.B: Complete rupture of the joint capsule during sports activities
options.C: Bacterial infection invading the bone marrow cavity directly
options.D: Gradual wear and tear of joint cartilage over time

explanation: Osteoarthritis comes from the gradual breakdown of protective cartilage, leading to bone rubbing on bone, pain, and stiffness. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T6#GNS121_U3_T6_h8)
